teaser: A woman sits and thinks. In 1905 that was enough to change sculpture.
review_notes:
IMAGE: the photo shows a bronze cast in the Carrousel/Tuileries garden in Paris, seen from behind under snow. The Musée d'Orsay owns the marble version (carved 1923 to 1927). The face and front of the figure are not visible, so only two interactive blocks point at large shapes.
Maillol's age (43) at the 1905 Salon d'Automne: born December 1861.
Original title 'Woman' at the 1905 Salon and the later title 'The Mediterranean': verify.
André Gide's comment is paraphrased from 'Elle est belle, elle ne signifie rien; c'est une oeuvre silencieuse'.
Harry Kessler's stone commission (now in Winterthur) and Clotilde Maillol as model: verify.
1964 gift by Dina Vierny with André Malraux: 'about twenty' bronzes (often given as 18).
Identification of the background group as Maillol's Three Nymphs is from the photo.

lesson.text: Forty-three. That is how old Aristide Maillol was when he showed this figure, his first large sculpture, in Paris in 1905. Until a few years earlier he had been a painter and a designer of tapestries.

His eyes had forced the change. Weaving tiny colored threads strained them so badly that he had to stop. He began to shape wood and clay by hand instead, in his home village of Banyuls, on the Mediterranean coast near Spain.

He worked on this seated woman for about five years, changing an arm, moving a leg, trying it again. What was he hunting for? Not a face or a story. In this photo you see the figure from behind, and it still tells you the answer.
Read the figure as a builder would: as a set of supports.

lines.label: A closed shape
lines.text: Head at the top, a foot and a hand at the corners. Nothing sticks out. The whole body fits inside one compact, stable form.

lines.label: The pillar
lines.text: One arm drops straight down to the base and props the body up like a column.

lines.label: The stack
lines.text: On the other side, head rests on hand, elbow rests on the raised knee, knee stands on the ground. Each part carries the one above.

lesson.text: So that was the goal: a body arranged like architecture, calm and balanced from every side, the back as worked out as the front. Maillol said he was looking for it the way one looks for the right proportions of a house.
The writer André Gide saw it in 1905 and summed it up in a line that became famous. She is beautiful, he wrote, and she means nothing: it is a silent work.

“Means nothing” was praise. Sculpture at the time was full of drama. The giant of the day, Auguste Rodin, made bodies that twist, suffer and reach. Maillol's woman does none of that. She simply sits, heavy and at peace.
Maillol removed the story from sculpture and kept only the form: simple volumes, balance, stillness. Much of modern sculpture starts from that choice.

Even the title came afterward. In 1905 it was shown simply as “Woman.” Maillol later called it The Mediterranean, after the sunlit, classical world he felt in it. A German collector, Count Harry Kessler, ordered a stone version straight away.

The marble in the Musée d'Orsay was ordered by the French state in 1923, and Maillol took about four years to finish it. The bronze in this photo sits outdoors in the gardens beside the Louvre, where snow and moss are free to settle on it.
She is not alone out there. In 1964 Maillol's last model, Dina Vierny, gave the French state about twenty of his bronzes for this garden. One of them is hiding in the distance of this very photo.
Far away, another group of Maillol's bronze women is standing in the snow. Where?

spots.title: Three more Maillols
spots.text: Three standing nudes on a low base, tiny at this distance. They are just as full and quiet as the seated woman, with the same weight on the ground.

lesson.text: Come back to the snow on her shoulders. A person would brush it off and hurry home. She stays, head on her hand, as she has since 1905. What do you think she is thinking about? Maillol made sure nobody could ever say.

quiz.question: What did Maillol do before turning to sculpture?
quiz.explanation: Eye strain from tapestry work pushed him toward sculpture.

quiz.question: What did André Gide admire in the figure?
options: That it is beautiful and means nothing
quiz.explanation: Gide called it a silent work, and meant it as praise.

quiz.question: How does the figure differ from Rodin's sculptures?
options: It is calm and still where his are dramatic
quiz.explanation: Maillol dropped drama and kept balanced, quiet volumes.

quiz.question: Under what title was the work first shown in 1905?
quiz.explanation: The name The Mediterranean was given later.

facts.text: Maillol was already past forty when he showed his first large sculpture.
facts.explanation: He was forty-three at the 1905 exhibition.

facts.text: The Musée d'Orsay version is made of bronze.
facts.explanation: The Orsay version is marble, ordered by the French state in 1923.

facts.text: The figure illustrates a scene from a famous Greek myth.
facts.explanation: It tells no story at all, which is exactly what Gide praised.
